newsitem.title: USA: Tip-off leads L.A. police to suspected Cosby killer.
newsitem.headline: Tip-off leads L.A. police to suspected Cosby killer.

text.p: Police acting on a tip-off from a tabloid newspaper charged an 18-year-old Russian emigre on Thursday with murdering the only son of entertainer Bill Cosby during a botched robbery.
Los Angeles police chief Willie Williams said the killing of Ennis Cosby did not appear to be either racially motivated or the work of a Russian organised crime gang.
Williams told reporters the suspect, Mikhail Markhasev, was born in the former Soviet Union but had lived in the United States for eight years.
"Even though he is of Russian origin, there are no indications that there is any Russian Mafia gang or any Russian Mafia tie at all," Williams said.
"It appears that robbery was the motive; it was happenstance," Williams said.
Cosby, 27, was gunned down in the early hours of Jan. 16 while changing a tire on his luxury Mercedes car by the side of a southern California freeway.
At the time of the murder, police said there was no indication anything had been stolen from Cosby, leading to speculation the graduate student may have been set up.
However, Williams said the evidence suggested the murder was a random crime.
"The examination of the tire of Mr. Cosby's car has not revealed anything that would indicate that there was any intentional flattening or intentional damage caused to the tire," he said.
The suspect was charged with one count of murder and was expected to be arraigned on Friday.
Markhasev, whom police sources said had an extensive juvenile crime record, closely resembled the composite sketch of the suspected killer.

The sketch was based on a description from the only known witness -- a woman Cosby called to help him change the flat tire. The woman said she drove off when she saw a man with a gun and when she returned Cosby was dead.
Two other people who were questioned by police on Wednesday were released.

Williams said police, acting on a tip-off from the tabloid National Enquirer, recovered the murder weapon and a knit cap "in an open area of Los Angeles." An earlier search of the area failed to turn up the gun or the cap.
Forensic tests showed the gun had fired the fatal shot.

Immediately after the murder, Bill Cosby challenged tabloids such as the Enquirer to put up a reward to find the killer. But later he and his wife Camille complained about the personal nature of tabloid news coverage of their son's death.

Ironically, the break in the case came as a result of the $100,000 reward the Enquirer offered. Executive editor David Perel said the tabloid had received hundreds of calls but that one sounded credible.
He said the caller seemed to know details about the case that had not been publicised, including information about the .38 calibre weapon.
The tipster said he was an acquaintance of a Russian who had told him he had shot a black man in the area where the murder occurred. The Enquirer passed the details on to police.

Williams acknowleged the tip was received in January and forwarded to the police department's elite robbery, homicide unit. Detectives from the unit gathered evidence and executed at least three search warrants, he said.

The Cosbys, who live in New York, said in a statement: "We want to thank the LAPD (Los Angeles Police Department). We realise how tough it must have been on them every day. We always had every hope that they would find the suspect and that jurisprudence would proceed."

Gavin de Becker, an adviser to the Cosby family who worked closely with police during the investigation, said in a statement the "caution and care" taken by the police "will make the journey from arrest to conviction a successful one."
